## The idea

Hold C underneath the notes of C major. Some notes settle into the drone. Some
seem to lean toward a neighbour. The pitches belong to one scale, yet they do
different work because the drone gives them a shared centre.

A note's position in a scale is its *scale degree*. Degree 1 is the *tonic*, the
pitch that feels like home. Degree 7 is the leading tone because it sits one
semitone below the tonic and presses upward. Degree 5, the dominant, is stable
enough to pause on while leaving the phrase open. I needed the drone to hear
these roles. An isolated B sounded like a pitch; B over C sounded like a request.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 72
use_synth :sine

define :play_phrase do |notes|
  notes.each do |pitch|
    play pitch, release: 0.38, amp: 0.8
    sleep 0.5
  end
end

c_major = scale(:c4, :major).to_a

in_thread do
  play :c3, sustain: 15.5, release: 0.5, amp: 0.45
end

[[6, 7], [3, 2], [4, 4], [1, 0]].each do |from, to|
  play c_major[from], release: 0.7
  sleep 1
  play c_major[to], release: 0.9
  sleep 2
end

stem = [:c4, :e4, :g4, :a4, :g4, :e4]
[:f4, :g4, :b4, :c5].each do |ending|
  play_phrase stem + [ending, ending]
  sleep 1
end
```

The first pair, B to C, makes the clearest arrival. F to E also relaxes, though
with less force. G repeated over the drone feels balanced and unfinished. The
four versions of the phrase change only their last pitch. Their different
degrees make one sound closed while the others keep the boundary porous.

## Change one thing

1. Replace the C drone with `:a2` while leaving the melody untouched. The notes
   now orbit A, and their roles change. Listen to C become a colour inside A
   minor rather than the point of arrival.
2. Change the B ending to `:bb4`. The pitch now sits a whole tone below C. Hear
   how reducing the half-step weakens the upward pull.
3. Raise the final G to `:g5`. It remains degree 5, yet register alters its
   weight. Decide whether the high dominant sounds more open or more final than
   the lower one.

## Why it works

Scale degree is an index interpreted relative to a tonic. The same MIDI number
can have another degree after the tonal centre changes. This resembles an offset
inside a data structure: the raw value is less informative than its position in
the current context.

Several forces combine. Small melodic distance encourages motion to a neighbour.
The semitone from degree 7 to 8 is especially tight. The tonic drone also shares
overtones with several scale notes, so degrees differ in roughness and stability.
Repeated musical use strengthens those expectations. No single rule assigns a
complete stability score, which is why listening over one fixed drone is useful.

The phrase experiment controls its variables. Rhythm, synth, register, and first
six notes stay fixed. The ending becomes the input under test. A longer melody
would hide the effect behind other changes. Here the degree has nowhere to hide.

## Take it further

Create a hash that maps degrees 1 through 7 to your own tension rating from 0 to
5. Write a program that plays each degree over a tonic drone in a shuffled order,
prints its number after a two-beat pause, and then resolves it by the route you
chose. Seed the shuffle with `use_random_seed 42`. Your finished exercise must
cover every degree once and keep the drone unchanged throughout.
